questions.problem: Evaluate the gradient of $g(x,y)$ at the point $({e}^{2},1)$ if $g(x,y)=(x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =1\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})+(x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}+1+\frac{y}{x} \\ {g}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x+y)(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =1\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})+(x+y)\cdot (-2y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}-2xy-2{y}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x-3{y}^{2}-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the gradient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),\,{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}+1+\frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x-3{y}^{2}-2xy⟩ \\ ∇g({e}^{2},1) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-{1}^{2}+1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})-3\cdot {1}^{2}-2\cdot {e}^{2}\cdot 1⟩ \\  & =⟨2+{e}^{-2},-1-2{e}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y)=2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j.$

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y)=0:$ 

$$
2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,i+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j=0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j
$$

So, by equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j,$ we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2(x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=0 \\ 2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2y & =0 \\ y & =0,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y=0,$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$

- For $y=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

Therefore, $∇h(x,y)=0,$ for $0\le y<\pi ,$ at two points: $(1,0)$ and $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2y-x=0 \\ 2x+y=0\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}+0-\frac{1}{z{x}^{2}}-0 \\  & =-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}+0-0 \\  & =-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{zx}-z) \\  & =0+0-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}x}-1 \\  & =-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k.$ 

Now, we solve $∇f(x,y,z)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}\,i-\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}\,j-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}\,k & =0\text{ }i+0\text{ }j+0\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the coefficient of $i$, $j$, and $k$, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{{x}^{2}yz}=0 \\ -\frac{1+x}{x{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=-1.$ Substituting these into the third equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1+{z}^{2}x}{{z}^{2}x} & =0 \\ -\frac{1+{z}^{2}(-1)}{{z}^{2}(-1)} & =0 \\ 1-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into the first equation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z+y}{(-1)^{2}yz} & =0 \\ z+y & =0 \\ y & =-z\end{aligned}
$$

When $z=1,$ we have $y=-1$ and when $z=-1,$ we have $y=1.$

Hence, $∇f(x,y,z)=0$ at two points: $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(-1,1,-1).$

$$
∇[fh]=h∇f+f∇h.

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)h(x,y)] & =h(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇h(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j)+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j) \\  & =\frac{y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\frac{x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j+\frac{x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j+\frac{x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{y+x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,i+\frac{y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})-x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}((y+x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}))i+(y\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})-x)j).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y)$ if $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$ and $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=f\,∇\,g+g\,∇\,f
$$

First, we calculate the first order partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y})={e}^{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j={e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\text{ }j=2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =({e}^{x+y})(2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j)+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})({e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =2x{e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+2y{e}^{x+y}\text{ }j+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }i+({x}^{2}+2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{x+y}\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $\nabla f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,\pi)$ given that $f(x,y) = (x - y)\cos y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y-(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡y+(x-y)\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{ }j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the gradient at the specified point, we substitute $(x,y)= (1,\pi)$ into the above, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(1,\pi ) & ={f}_{x}(1,\pi )\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(1,\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \text{ }i-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +(1-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\nabla g(x,y,z)$   at $(2,-1,3)$ if $g(x,y,z) = x^2 + xyz.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =2x+yz \\ {g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xz \\  & =xz \\ {g}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+xyz) \\  & =0+xy \\  & =xy\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & ={g}_{x}(x,y,z)\text{ }i+{g}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{g}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =(2x+yz)\text{ }i+(xz)\text{ }j+(xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇g(2,-1,3) & =(2(2)+(-1)(3))\text{ }i+2(3)\text{ }j+2(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =1\text{ }i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =i+6\text{ }j-2\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y-4)\ln (x-2),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\frac{y-4}{x-2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y-4}{x-2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x-2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \  \mathbf i + 0\ \mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{x-2}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y-4=0,$ which means $y=4.$  From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x-2)=0,$ which means that $x=3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf  0$ at the point $(3,4).$

tutorials.problem:
The **gradient** of a multivariable function is analogous to the derivative of a single-variable function.

For a function $f(x,y)$ whose partial derivatives exist at a point $(x,y),$ the **gradient vector** is denoted $\nabla f(x,y)$ and can be found by computing the vector of partial derivatives:

 

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f (x,y) =  \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \mathbf j
                              
}
$$

tutorials.title: The Gradient of a Function of More Than Two Variables
tutorials.content:
For a function of three variables $f(x,y,z)$, the gradient of $f$ is given by the vector  

 

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla \! f (x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z)\ \mathbf i + f_y (x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z (x,y,z)\ \mathbf k.
                             
}
$$

 

For a function $f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$ of $n$ variables, its gradient is usually given as a column vector:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14252648/assets/21e05d85506da576e293bce86b1ca98f4f5b101c49b0591a49d80d2a4b8bfcc1.svg)

tutorials.name: Properties of the Gradient
tutorials.problem:
Since the gradient of a function of several variables is made up of partial derivatives, we can expect it to have properties that are similar to partial derivatives.

Assume that $f$ and $g$ are functions whose first-order partial derivatives exist and are continuous on some open domain, and that $a,b,$ and $c$ are real constants. Then, the gradient has the following properties:

- Constant rule:  $\nabla c = \mathbf 0$

- Linearity: $\nabla (af + bg) = a \nabla\! f + b\nabla\! g$

- Product Rule: $\nabla(fg) = g \nabla\! f + f \nabla\! g$

- Quotient Rule: $\nabla \left( \dfrac{f}{g}\right) = \dfrac{ g \nabla\! f - f \nabla\! g}{g^2}$
